relationships.description: Connects Optimistic Concurrency Control to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

concept.tagline: Lock-free concurrency control that validates a monotonic version or ETag at commit time to prevent lost updates.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of Optimistic Concurrency Control—from why holding DB locks over HTTP fails to how versioned CAS and `If-Match` headers scale under low contention.

spark.summary: A lock-free concurrency pattern that lets readers and writers proceed without blocking, validating at commit time via a version number or ETag that no one else modified the record.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use atomic compare-and-swap (`UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` or HTTP `If-Match`) when conflicts are rare (<5%), and pair retries with exponential backoff and full jitter.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Formalized by Kung and Robinson (1981), **Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)** bets that conflicts are the exception.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Two Concurrent Writers Resolved by Monotonic Version (Worker A -> Orders DB (v=42) -> Worker B); HTTP If-Match -> PostgreSQL MVCC Version Check (PATCH + If-Match -> API Gateway -> WAL + Tuple Lock -> 1 Row -> 200 OK).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Match the concurrency control mechanism to conflict probability and multi-row invariants. A REST API serves `ETag: "42"` on `GET /orders/9001`.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Compare OCC with pessimistic locking, database isolation levels, and retry-storm prevention.

learningJourney.title: What is Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)
learningJourney.explanation:
Formalized by Kung and Robinson (1981), **Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)** bets that conflicts are the exception. Instead of acquiring locks before reading, a transaction runs in three phases: **Read** (fetch record + monotonic `version` or `ETag`), **Modify** (compute new state in memory), and **Validate/Write** (execute an atomic compare-and-swap such as `UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2`).

If 0 rows are affected—or DynamoDB raises `ConditionalCheckFailedException` or HTTP returns `412 Precondition Failed`—the writer aborts and retries or prompts the user.

UPDATE SET v=43 WHERE v=42 (0 rows!)

sectionDiagram.summary: Zero read locks are held; Worker B detects the concurrent write atomically at commit time instead of silently overwriting Worker A.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why we need OCC (and why wall-clock timestamps fail)
learningJourney.explanation: Holding database row locks across network calls or human think-time (like editing a document or checking out a cart) stalls concurrent users and saturates connection pools. OCC eliminates lock waiting on reads. Crucially, **never use `updated_at` wall-clock timestamps** for OCC comparisons: NTP drift and sub-millisecond collisions silently cause lost updates.

ideas.title: Full Jitter Stops Retry Storms
ideas.description: If 100 workers collide on `v=42` and retry in a tight loop, DB load multiplies 10x. Cap attempts (3–5) and sleep `random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))`.

ideas.title: Keep Side Effects Outside the Retry Loop
ideas.description: Never charge a credit card inside an OCC loop; if the DB CAS fails and retries, you double-charge the customer. Use a Transactional Outbox instead.

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without OCC under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Where OCC excels (and where Pessimistic Locking wins)
learningJourney.explanation: OCC shines under low-to-moderate contention (<5–10% conflict rate) and stateless HTTP APIs; high-contention hot keys need pessimistic locks or atomic increments.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Low Contention (<5% conflicts) & Stateless REST
benefits: 1-RTT writes with zero lock wait; works cleanly across disconnected HTTP calls via `ETag` + `If-Match`.
costs: Callers must handle `409 Conflict` / `412 Precondition Failed` and retry or merge.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Distributed NoSQL (DynamoDB, etcd, K8s)
benefits: Native `ConditionExpression` and `resourceVersion` CAS without cross-node lock managers.
costs: Read-modify-write requires an extra read RTT if the caller does not already hold the latest version.

comparison.choice: Avoid: Flash-Sale Hot Keys (>20% conflict rate)
benefits: Use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, atomic SQL `SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty >= 1`, or a single-writer queue.
costs: At 30%+ conflicts, OCC wastes more DB IOPS failing and re-reading than queuing behind a lock.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: How OCC Retry Loops and `If-Match` APIs are implemented
learningJourney.explanation: Assert `rows_affected == 1` on every SQL CAS update (many ORMs silently succeed on 0 rows unless `@Version` throws `OptimisticLockingFailureException`), enforce `If-Match` on `PUT`/`PATCH` (returning `428 Precondition Required` if omitted), and bound retries with full jitter.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```python
import random, time

def update_with_occ(repo, order_id: str, cmd, max_attempts: int = 4, base_ms: int = 20, cap_ms: int = 400):
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        record = repo.get(order_id)
        updated = record.apply_change(cmd)
        # Executes: UPDATE orders SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = %s AND version = %s
        if repo.compare_and_swap(updated, expected_version=record.version):
            return updated
        sleep_ms = random.uniform(0, min(cap_ms, base_ms * (2 ** attempt)))
        time.sleep(sleep_ms / 1000.0)
    raise ConflictError("Max OCC retries exceeded")
```

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: OCC vs. Pessimistic Locking vs. Atomic Deltas
learningJourney.explanation: Match the concurrency control mechanism to conflict probability and multi-row invariants.

benefits: Zero deadlocks, zero lock-wait timeouts, and optimal throughput when conflicts < 5%.
costs: Throughput collapses under heavy hot-key contention due to wasted read-compute-abort cycles.

benefits: Predictable queuing under >20% contention and enforces multi-row invariants cleanly.
costs: Ties up DB connections while waiting and risks AB-BA deadlocks without canonical lock ordering.

benefits: Single SQL statement with no client read-modify-write round trip.
costs: Only works for simple arithmetic/append predicates, not complex multi-field business rules.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production example: HTTP `ETag` + PostgreSQL MVCC Version Guard
learningJourney.explanation: A REST API serves `ETag: "42"` on `GET /orders/9001`. Clients send `If-Match: "42"` on `PATCH`. PostgreSQL executes `UPDATE orders SET ..., version = 43 WHERE id = 9001 AND version = 42` using its MVCC tuple visibility; 0 affected rows maps cleanly to `412 Precondition Failed`.

sectionDiagram.title: HTTP If-Match -> PostgreSQL MVCC Version Check

cards.label: 1. Strict Precondition
cards.detail: Requests omitting If-Match receive 428 Precondition Required so old clients cannot silently clobber state.

cards.label: 2. Row-Level CAS
cards.detail: Postgres acquires a brief tuple lock only for the commit instant of the UPDATE statement.

cards.label: 3. Deterministic Status
cards.detail: 0 rows affected returns 412 Precondition Failed, never 500 Internal Server Error.

sectionDiagram.summary: MVCC + versioned WHERE clauses enforce lock-free safety across disconnected HTTP clients.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is using a client- or server-generated `updated_at` timestamp unsafe as the sole version check in Optimistic Concurrency Control?

options.text: Clock skew across nodes or two writes within the same timestamp resolution can pass the check and cause silent lost updates
options.feedback: Correct: always use a strictly monotonic integer (`version = version + 1`) or storage-assigned revision/ETag.

options.text: Databases cannot index timestamp columns in a WHERE clause
options.feedback: Timestamps are indexable, but they are not strictly monotonic across concurrent writers.

options.text: Timestamps force PostgreSQL to upgrade to a full table lock
options.feedback: The issue is ABA/collision lost updates, not table locks.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
